title: The Evaluation, Diagnosis, and Management of Ovarian Cysts, Masses, and Their Complications in Fetuses, Infants, Children, and Adolescents
study_design: Comprehensive review of the evaluation, diagnosis, and management of ovarian cysts and masses by pediatric age group; no formal study methodology is described.

population.description: Female fetuses, infants, children, and adolescents with ovarian cysts or masses.

condition_or_topic: Ovarian cysts, masses, and related complications in fetuses, infants, children, and adolescents
clinical_background: Ovarian lesions account for most abdominal masses in female children and range from functional cysts to malignant tumors. Cysts constitute 60% of pediatric ovarian lesions, whereas ovarian neoplasms occur at a rate of 2.6 cases per 100,000 girls per year. Malignancy is reported in 3–8% of adnexal masses and accounts for 1–2% of pediatric cancers. The frequency, presentation, and tumor types vary with age: germ cell tumors predominate among ovarian neoplasms in children and adolescents, while functional cysts are more frequent around the fetal/neonatal and perimenarchal periods. Assessment focuses on the likelihood of malignancy because benign and malignant lesions require substantially different management. Ultrasound is the initial imaging modality; further imaging and serum tumor markers can inform evaluation. When surgery is needed, preserving ovarian tissue and future fertility is an important consideration.
objectives: Provide a comprehensive overview of the evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment of ovarian masses in pediatric patients.
Describe how lesion characteristics and management differ across age subgroups.
interpretation: The review concludes that pediatric ovarian cysts and masses require an age-specific, individualized approach that generally favors surveillance and preservation of ovarian tissue. Intervention is reserved for symptomatic lesions, complications, or findings concerning for malignancy. Management should account for both physical and psychological outcomes.
clinical_implications: Because benign and malignant ovarian lesions require substantially different management, assessment of malignancy risk is central to clinical decision-making.
Spontaneous resolution is common among functional cysts, particularly in fetuses and infants, although the likelihood of regression in infants decreases as cyst size increases.
Neither normal Doppler flow nor the absence of elevated tumor markers excludes the respective concerns of ovarian torsion and malignancy. Elevated tumor markers also occur in benign tumors.

Loss of an ovary may affect the quantity of ovarian reserve even when its quality, as reflected by pregnancy rates, is comparable. Preserving ovarian function also supports pubertal development and hormonal balance.

An ovarian neoplasm identified during childhood can be an initial indication of a cancer predisposition syndrome, with implications for genetic counseling and surveillance of the patient and her relatives.
Diagnosis and surgery can have psychological effects, particularly in adolescents, alongside surgical, hormonal, and fertility-related consequences.
practice_implications: Use ultrasound as the initial imaging assessment of pediatric adnexal lesions, incorporating Doppler assessment where appropriate. Consider MRI or CT when ultrasound does not clarify the lesion’s origin or when a mass is large or suspected to be malignant.

Assess possible malignancy using clinical presentation, imaging, laboratory findings, and histology rather than relying on tumor markers alone. Surgical removal followed by histopathological assessment establishes the definitive diagnosis.

Monitor fetal ovarian cysts carefully for growth, torsion, and compression of abdominal organs. Percutaneous aspiration has been proposed for cysts ≥40 mm or growth ≥10 mm per week, whereas expectant care is also advocated because simple cysts may resolve; the preferred approach remains uncertain. A fetal ovarian cyst should not itself change delivery timing or method.

After birth, monitor ovarian cysts with ultrasound every 4–6 weeks. For cysts that grow or remain for 4 months or more, continued surveillance, aspiration, and cystectomy are all described as reasonable options. Aspiration may be considered for an uncomplicated neonatal cyst ≥ 6 cm that has not regressed by four months; a recurrent cyst may be aspirated again or removed surgically.

For asymptomatic prepubertal girls with ovarian cysts, favor observation and counsel the child and parents about torsion symptoms requiring prompt emergency assessment. Consider surgical exploration for cysts ≥ 9 cm, sonographic features concerning for a tumor, torsion, or acute rupture with bleeding and hemodynamic instability.

In adolescents, follicular cysts usually resolve within eight weeks. Monophasic combination estrogen/progestin OCPs containing ≥ 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol are commonly recommended to suppress ovulation and prevent a new functional cyst. Persistence for ≥3 months, size ≥ 6 cm, pelvic pain, or urinary frequency are indications for laparoscopic cystectomy or aspiration, although selected simple cysts measuring 6 to 12 cm can be monitored. Cystectomy is usually favored over aspiration because recurrence after aspiration is frequent.

For an asymptomatic adolescent with a corpus luteum cyst, observation for three months is recommended; monophasic combination estrogen/progestin OCPs with ≥ 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol are also prescribed. Cystectomy alone is rarely needed, but persistent or non-involuting cysts should be removed while preserving ovarian tissue.

When surgery is needed for a benign ovarian lesion, prioritize ovarian-sparing cystectomy or tumor enucleation rather than oophorectomy where feasible. Aspiration of cyst contents alone is not recommended as definitive management because it supplies no tissue for histopathology and fluid cytology cannot reliably exclude malignancy.

Use a minimally invasive ovarian-sparing approach where feasible. Strong suspicion of malignancy or intraoperative confirmation on frozen section warrants a different surgical approach; suspected or confirmed malignancy requires appropriate staging.

Diagnose and treat suspected ovarian torsion without delay. Surgical visualization establishes the diagnosis; laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian preservation is the preferred initial approach, even when the ovary appears blue or black. Reserve oophorectomy for rare cases of extensive necrosis or a nonviable gelatinous appearance. Oophoropexy has been proposed for patients at high risk of recurrence.

Consider tubal torsion when compatible findings are present, since prompt surgical detorsion can prevent irreversible tubal injury. If a paraovarian cyst has twisted, excise it carefully to protect ovarian and tubal function.

For rupture of a hemorrhagic ovarian cyst with self-limiting bleeding, monitor serial hemoglobin and hematocrit. Stabilize a hemodynamically unstable patient before surgery; laparotomy is recommended only when pediatric laparoscopic expertise is unavailable or instability cannot be corrected.

Arrange postoperative follow-up for pediatric ovarian tumors every 3 to 6 months during the first 2 to 3 years and then annually for up to 5 years or longer. Include examination and relevant tumor markers, with ultrasound or, if needed, CT or MRI when symptoms or findings are concerning. Address complications, hormonal function, fertility, and psychological needs.

Treat children and adolescents with ovarian masses in specialized centers through a multidisciplinary team that includes pediatric gynecologists and surgeons and, when malignancy is suspected, pediatric oncologists. Provide psychosocial support while avoiding unnecessary oophorectomy.
open_questions: The optimal treatment strategy for fetal ovarian cysts remains disputed between aspiration and expectant management.
The clinical role of HE4 and CEA in pediatric ovarian tumors remains insufficiently defined.
The diagnostic accuracy and clinical usefulness of ROMA in pediatric patients remain to be established.
future_directions: Further research is needed to determine the diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility of ROMA for pediatric ovarian tumors.
Clarifying the role of HE4 could improve understanding of pediatric ovarian tumor biology.

main_conclusion: The authors favor individualized monitoring and conservative management of pediatric ovarian cysts and masses, with intervention for symptoms or concerning findings. They recommend care by multidisciplinary teams in specialized centers to avoid unnecessary oophorectomy and protect ovarian function, fertility, and psychological well-being.
narrative_summary: This comprehensive review examines the diagnosis and management of ovarian cysts, masses, and complications from fetal life through adolescence, emphasizing differences between age groups. Ovarian cysts account for 60% of pediatric ovarian lesions; true neoplasms occur at 2.6 cases per 100,000 girls per year, and 3–8% of adnexal masses are malignant. Ultrasound is the initial imaging test, with MRI or CT used when findings are inconclusive or malignancy is suspected. Clinical findings, imaging, and laboratory markers inform malignancy risk, but tumor markers alone cannot confirm or exclude cancer. Many fetal and infant cysts regress spontaneously. Proposed fetal aspiration for cysts ≥40 mm or growth ≥10 mm per week remains controversial, while ultrasound surveillance after birth is recommended every 4–6 weeks. In adolescents, persistent cysts for ≥3 months, size ≥ 6 cm, pelvic pain, or urinary frequency are indications for laparoscopic cystectomy or aspiration; cystectomy is generally preferred because aspiration has a high recurrence rate. Suspected torsion requires prompt surgical assessment, and normal Doppler flow does not exclude it. When feasible, surgery should preserve ovarian tissue; oophorectomy is reserved for specified circumstances, including malignancy or an unsalvageable ovary. The authors advocate individualized, multidisciplinary care in specialized centers.

main_findings.description: Prepubertal ovarian cysts are uncommon in the absence of an associated condition; observational studies indicate that cysts up to 9 cm in diameter usually resolve without intervention.
main_findings.context: Resolution finding is attributed to observational studies cited by the review.

main_findings.description: Follicular cysts in adolescents generally disappear without intervention within eight weeks.
main_findings.context: Course described from cited literature.

main_findings.description: Some simple ovarian cysts measuring 6 to 12 cm in adolescents may resolve spontaneously.
main_findings.context: The review states that selected patients with cysts in this size range can be monitored.

main_findings.description: A neonate with an abdominal mass had a necrotic, twisted ovarian cyst; after decompression, obvious ovarian necrosis led to laparoscopic salpingo-oophorectomy.
main_findings.context: Illustrative case of a 7-day-old neonate.

main_findings.description: An adolescent with recurrent brief episodes of abdominal pain had a nonperfused right ovarian mass; surgery showed torsion and partial necrosis, and histopathology identified a mature teratoma.
main_findings.context: Illustrative case of a 13-year-old adolescent whose symptoms had lasted about a week.

main_findings.description: An adolescent with a large right ovarian cyst underwent laparoscopic cystectomy with ovarian preservation; histopathology showed a simple ovarian cyst.
main_findings.context: Illustrative case of a 14-year-old girl; the cyst compressed surrounding structures.

main_findings.description: Ovarian tumors, whether benign or malignant, represent a small fraction of tumors in children and adolescents.
main_findings.context: Estimate from cited literature.

main_findings.description: Germ cell tumors constitute a substantial proportion of ovarian tumors in children and adolescents.
main_findings.context: Estimate from cited literature.

main_findings.context: Classification proportions reported from cited literature.

main_findings.description: Mature and immature teratomas together account for most ovarian germ cell tumors and can affect both ovaries.

main_findings.context: The first value is their share of ovarian germ cell tumors; the second is the reported frequency of bilateral disease.

main_findings.description: YSTs are described as the most common malignant ovarian germ cell tumors in children, whereas dysgerminomas are the most common malignant entity in adolescence.
main_findings.context: Age-specific characterization and bilaterality estimate from cited literature.

main_findings.description: An adolescent with bilateral ovarian masses underwent laparotomy and bilateral cystectomy; histopathology identified a mature teratoma, and tumor markers were not elevated.
main_findings.context: Illustrative case of an 11-year-old girl.

main_findings.description: An adolescent with primary amenorrhea and tumors in both gonads underwent bilateral laparoscopic adnexectomy; histopathology identified bilateral gonadoblastoma with dysgerminoma components.
main_findings.context: Illustrative case of a 17-year-old with a female phenotype; neither excised specimen contained gonadal tissue.

main_findings.description: Epithelial ovarian tumors are uncommon during childhood.
main_findings.context: Estimate from cited literature.

main_findings.description: Epithelial ovarian tumors can involve both ovaries.
main_findings.context: Estimate from cited literature.

main_findings.description: An adolescent with abdominal distension had an intraperitoneal mass associated with the right ovary that compressed the pancreas and abdominal aorta; surgical exploration identified a mature cystic teratoma with adenocarcinoma foci.
main_findings.context: Illustrative case of a 14-year-old girl.

main_findings.description: Sex cord-stromal tumors are rare in children and adolescents and account for a reported share of ovarian malignancies.
main_findings.context: Estimate from cited literature.

main_findings.description: Meta-analyses of observational studies found that assessing gray-scale morphology together with color Doppler performed better than assessing morphology, spectral Doppler, or color Doppler individually.
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to cited meta-analyses; no pooled effect or statistical measure is provided.

main_findings.description: The review reports that normal Doppler flow cannot exclude ovarian torsion.
main_findings.context: Flow may persist with partial vascular occlusion, intermittent torsion, or collateral circulation.

main_findings.description: Tumor-marker findings alone cannot definitively establish or exclude malignancy in pediatric ovarian tumors.
main_findings.context: Benign tumors may have elevated markers, and malignant tumors may lack marker elevation.

main_findings.description: Despite recommendations to preserve the ovary when treating benign pediatric ovarian tumors, a substantial proportion of these lesions are treated by oophorectomy.
main_findings.context: Rate reported from cited literature for benign ovarian tumors in children and adolescents.

main_findings.description: Ovarian torsion occurs across pediatric age groups and may arise with or without adnexal pathology.
main_findings.context: Incidence reported from cited literature.

main_findings.description: Many ovaries, including some that appear blue or black, retain function after detorsion.
main_findings.context: Outcome described from cited literature; no preservation rate is provided.

main_findings.description: An adolescent with acute abdominal pain and vomiting underwent exploratory laparotomy and left adnexectomy after a ruptured, torsed ovarian tumor was found; histopathology identified a ruptured cystic mature teratoma.
main_findings.context: Illustrative case of a 14-year-old girl.

main_findings.description: An adolescent with a paraovarian cyst and left adnexal torsion underwent laparoscopic salpingo-oophorectomy because the ovary and fallopian tube were visibly gangrenous; histopathology identified a necrotic paraovarian cyst and ovarian gangrene.
main_findings.context: Illustrative case of a 15-year-old girl; symptoms began five days before surgery.

main_findings.description: Following oophorectomy, patients with one remaining ovary had less ovarian reserve by quantity but comparable reserve quality, including pregnancy rates, relative to patients with two ovaries.
main_findings.context: Comparison reported from cited literature; the review provides no numerical effect estimate.

drugs_and_therapies.name: monophasic combination estrogen/progestin oral contraceptive pills (OCPs)
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Inhibit the ovarian-hypothalamic axis and can stop ovulation and the formation of a new functional cyst.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Commonly recommended for adolescent follicular cysts and also prescribed for corpus luteum cysts; the stated formulation contains ≥ 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol.

drugs_and_therapies.name: ethinyl estradiol
drugs_and_therapies.context: Named component of the recommended adolescent OCPs formulation at ≥ 35 mcg.

drugs_and_therapies.name: observation
drugs_and_therapies.context: A conservative option for selected asymptomatic or potentially self-resolving cysts.

drugs_and_therapies.name: ultrasound observation
drugs_and_therapies.context: Recommended after birth for infant ovarian cysts every 4–6 weeks.

drugs_and_therapies.name: percutaneous aspiration
drugs_and_therapies.context: A proposed fetal cyst decompression option whose use is discussed alongside expectant management.

drugs_and_therapies.name: aspiration
drugs_and_therapies.context: Considered for selected neonatal or adolescent cysts; aspiration of cyst contents alone is not recommended as a substitute for histopathological assessment.

drugs_and_therapies.name: cystectomy
drugs_and_therapies.context: Removes a cyst while seeking to retain ovarian tissue.

drugs_and_therapies.name: laparoscopic cystectomy
drugs_and_therapies.context: A frequently preferred ovary-preserving surgical approach, including for persistent adolescent cysts.

drugs_and_therapies.name: bilateral cystectomy
drugs_and_therapies.context: Performed in the illustrated patient with bilateral mature teratomas.

drugs_and_therapies.name: enucleation of a solid tumor

drugs_and_therapies.name: laparoscopy
drugs_and_therapies.context: A minimally invasive approach favored for appropriate pediatric ovarian surgery.

drugs_and_therapies.name: laparotomy
drugs_and_therapies.context: An operative approach considered in selected circumstances, including certain large or concerning masses.

drugs_and_therapies.name: oophorectomy
drugs_and_therapies.context: Reserved for specified circumstances in which ovarian preservation is not feasible or malignancy is present.

drugs_and_therapies.name: partial oophorectomy
drugs_and_therapies.context: A less extensive option considered before oophorectomy for some benign neoplasms.

drugs_and_therapies.name: salpingo-oophorectomy
drugs_and_therapies.context: Performed in illustrated patients when ovarian necrosis or adnexal gangrene was evident.

drugs_and_therapies.name: bilateral laparoscopic adnexectomy

drugs_and_therapies.name: detorquation

drugs_and_therapies.name: surgical detorsion

drugs_and_therapies.name: oophoropexy

drugs_and_therapies.name: plication of the utero-ovarian ligament

drugs_and_therapies.name: laparoscopically guided minilaparotomy

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Most abdominal masses in girls originate in the ovaries and range from functional cysts to malignancies. Their frequency, presentation, and histology vary with age. Assessment focuses on malignancy risk because benign and malignant lesions require substantially different management. Ultrasound is the principal examination for size, location, and morphology; MRI or CT can provide further assessment when ultrasound is inconclusive or malignancy is suspected, particularly in older adolescents. Serum markers may help assess malignancy risk in older adolescents but are less useful in younger patients because normal values change during development. Many functional cysts, especially fetal and infant cysts, resolve without treatment. Large symptomatic cysts or suspected malignancy may warrant surgery, preferably an ovary-preserving laparoscopy or laparotomy. Torsion, rupture, and hemorrhage may require urgent surgery. Specialized centers can help prevent unnecessary oophorectomies. This review examines age-specific evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment of pediatric ovarian masses.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Ovarian lesions account for most abdominal masses in pediatric girls and span functional cysts through malignant tumors. Cysts constitute 60% of pediatric ovarian lesions. True neoplasms occur at 2.6 cases per 100,000 girls per year; 3–8% of adnexal masses are malignant, representing 1–2% of pediatric cancers. Neoplasms are grouped by origin into germ cell, sex cordstromal, and epithelial tumors. Incidence, causes, and presentation vary by age: germ cell tumors predominate among childhood and adolescent ovarian neoplasms, whereas epithelial tumors predominate in adults. Mature cystic teratomas are the most frequent tumor type, and dysgerminomas are described as the most frequent malignant ovarian neoplasm in the pediatric population. Functional cysts peak in the fetal/neonatal and perimenarchal periods, reflecting maternal gonadotropins or activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis. Ultrasound is the initial imaging choice; MRI offers additional soft-tissue detail without ionizing radiation. Imaging and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), and inhibin A and B contribute to malignancy-risk assessment. Pediatric surgery should favor fertility preservation, minimally invasive laparoscopy, and ovarian conservation when feasible. The review addresses evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment across pediatric age groups.

document_sections.heading: 2. Ovarian Cysts 2.1. Fetuses
document_sections.content: Fetal ovarian cysts are the most frequent abdominal cysts in female fetuses, occurring at 1:2500 and generally identified in the third trimester. They are usually functional or benign; increased fetal gonadotropins, maternal estrogens, and placental human chorionic gonadotropins are implicated. Cysts < 20 mm in diameter are considered physiological maturing follicles, whereas those > 20 mm are abnormal. Simple cysts are round, anechoic, unilocular, and thin-walled; complex cysts have thick walls, mixed echogenicity, fluid-debris levels, or internal septations. Identifying the organ of origin and surrounding anatomy helps distinguish these lesions from simple renal cysts, multicystic dysplastic kidneys, hydronephrosis, urachal cysts, hydrocolpos, enteric duplication cysts, meconium pseudocysts, choledochal cysts, lymphatic malformations, and cystic sacrococcygeal teratoma. MRI may be useful with maternal obesity, fetal malposition, or oligohydramnios. A daughter cyst is a small anechoic round structure within the main cyst and is a characteristic ultrasound finding. Usual ultrasound diagnostic criteria are female sex, a regular cystic structure away from the midline, and urinary and gastrointestinal tracts of normal appearance. Perinatal care prioritizes monitoring growth and changes to avoid torsion, ovarian necrosis, and compression of abdominal organs. Optimal treatment remains disputed: percutaneous aspiration has been suggested particularly for diameter ≥40 mm or growth ≥10 mm per week, while expectant care has also been advocated because spontaneous resolution is possible, especially for simple cysts. A fetal cyst should not change delivery timing or method because torsion risk, onset, and duration cannot be predicted.

document_sections.heading: 2.2. Infants
document_sections.content: Ovarian cysts often regress after birth, generally by 6 months or even 1 year of age. Spontaneous regression becomes less frequent as size increases, ranging from approximately 90% for cysts ≤ 2.9 cm to 20% for cysts ≥ 6 cm. Postnatal ultrasound surveillance is recommended every 4–6 weeks. If a cyst grows or remains for 4 months or more, further observation, aspiration, and cystectomy are all reasonable options. Aspiration can be considered for an uncomplicated neonatal cyst ≥ 6 cm that has not regressed by four months; recurrence can be managed with repeat aspiration or removal. Removal is usual for complex, symptomatic, or enlarging neonatal cysts. When operating, laparoscopy is recommended with maximal preservation of ovarian tissue. Torsion is the commonest infant complication, principally affecting rapidly growing cysts whose sonographic appearance changes; pedicle length appears more closely related to torsion risk than cyst size. An illustrated 7-day-old neonate had a necrotic ovarian cyst measuring 6 × 5 × 4 cm, with pedicle rotation of 720 degrees; after decompression, visible necrosis prompted laparoscopic salpingo-oophorectomy.

document_sections.heading: 2.3. Children
document_sections.content: Prepubertal cysts are uncommon without an associated condition because gonadotropin stimulation falls after the neonatal period and usually remains low until puberty. Associated conditions include idiopathic central precocious puberty, McCune Albright syndrome, thyroid disorders, and hormonally active ovarian tumors. Nevertheless, most simple childhood cysts result from an ovarian follicle failing to regress. A prepubertal cyst may be an incidental imaging finding or an asymptomatic mass with abdominal distension. Larger symptomatic cysts can produce persistent periumbilical or lower-quadrant pain, bloating, urinary frequency or retention, constipation, or fullness. Sudden severe pain generally suggests torsion, perforation, hemorrhage, or infarction. Ultrasound should distinguish ovarian cysts from paraovarian, mesothelial, and broad ligament cysts. Management depends on sonographic features and clinical findings. Observation is preferred for asymptomatic patients, alongside counseling children and parents about torsion symptoms so emergency care can be sought promptly. Prepubertal observational studies report that cysts up to 9 cm usually resolve spontaneously. Surgical exploration is indicated for diameter ≥ 9 cm because malignancy risk increases, tumor-suggestive ultrasound findings such as septations, increased solid tissue or calcification, torsion, or acute rupture with bleeding and hemodynamic instability.

document_sections.heading: 2.4. Adolescents
document_sections.content: Adolescent ovaries contain follicles at different stages. Most adolescent cysts are follicular, arising when a developing follicle neither ovulates nor involutes. Large cysts may cause urinary frequency, constipation, or lower abdominal pressure; torsion, rupture, and hemorrhage cause intense acute pain. The differential diagnosis includes obstructive genital anomalies, ovarian tumors, tubal disease, uterine masses, and urinary or gastrointestinal conditions. Ultrasound is the first imaging examination. Follicular cysts generally resolve within eight weeks. Monophasic combined estrogen/progestin oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) with ≥ 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol are commonly recommended to inhibit the ovarian-hypothalamic axis, suppress ovulation, and prevent new functional cysts. Persistence for ≥3 months, size ≥ 6 cm, pelvic pain, or urinary frequency are indications for laparoscopic cystectomy or aspiration, although some simple cysts measuring 6 to 12 cm resolve and can be monitored safely in selected patients. Cystectomy is usually preferred over aspiration because aspiration has a high recurrence rate. For asymptomatic corpus luteum cysts, observation for three months is recommended; monophasic combined estrogen/progestin OCPs containing ≥ 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol are also prescribed, and cystectomy alone is seldom justified. Persistent or non-involuting cysts should undergo cystectomy with preservation of ovarian tissue. One illustrated 13-year-old had about a week of brief recurrent cramping; imaging showed a nonperfused right ovarian solid-cystic mass measuring 9.1 × 8.8 cm, and surgery identified torsion with partial necrosis and a mature teratoma on histology. Another illustrated 14-year-old had intermittent pain, anorexia, and a palpable right ovarian cyst measuring 16.2 × 14.6 cm that compressed nearby structures; after aspiration of 2 L of clear contents, ovarian-sparing laparoscopic cystectomy yielded a simple cyst.

document_sections.heading: 3. Ovarian Masses
document_sections.content: Most childhood ovarian masses are functional cysts or benign tumors, but timely diagnosis affects outcomes in malignancy. A mass can be discovered incidentally or cause abdominal pain or enlargement, a palpable abdominal or pelvic mass, nausea, vomiting, fullness, constipation, lower abdominal pressure, urinary frequency or retention, precocious puberty with virilization, menstrual irregularities, or a paraneoplastic or autoimmune syndrome. Presentation depends on age, size, and pathology. Benign and malignant ovarian tumors together represent 1–2% of childhood and adolescent tumors, occurring at roughly 2.6 per 100,000 girls annually. Around 10–20% of surgically treated ovarian tumors are malignant. Bilaterality, fixation with irregular margins, ascites, and precocious puberty are more often associated with malignant than benign tumors.

document_sections.heading: 3.1. Germ Cell Tumors
document_sections.content: Germ cell tumors account for 35–45% of ovarian tumors in children and adolescents; examples include mature teratomas, immature teratomas, yolk sac tumors (YSTs), gonadoblastomas, dysgerminomas, embryonal carcinoma, non-gestational choriocarcinoma, and mixed germ cell tumors. They reflect abnormal germ-cell differentiation. Among germ cell tumors (GCTs), 80% are benign and 20% malignant. Mature and immature teratomas make up approximately 80% of ovarian GCTs and are bilateral in 5% of cases. YSTs are the commonest malignant ovarian GCTs in children, whereas dysgerminomas are the commonest malignant entity in adolescents and are bilateral in 10% of cases. Gonadoblastoma is uncommon and occurs in girls with dysgenetic gonads. An illustrated 11-year-old had abdominal enlargement, pain, nausea, and bilateral solid-cystic masses resembling dermoids, measuring left 13 cm and right 5 cm; tumor markers were not increased. Laparotomy and bilateral cystectomy were performed, and histology showed mature teratoma. An illustrated 17-year-old evaluated for primary amenorrhea had a female phenotype, karyotype 46, XY, and tumors in both gonads, with the left resembling a testis and the right an ovary. Following diagnosis of a disorder of sexual development (DSD), bilateral laparoscopic adnexectomy revealed bilateral gonadoblastoma with dysgerminoma components and no gonadal tissue in either specimen. Staging was TNM: T1bNXMX; Figo classification: 1b.

document_sections.heading: 3.2. Epithelial Tumors
document_sections.content: Epithelial tumors, including serous and mucinous cystadenomas, account for less than 20% of childhood ovarian tumors and are unusual before puberty. These tumors may be benign, malignant, or have low malignant potential. Up to 20% involve both ovaries. Malignant forms, including cystadenocarcinoma and undifferentiated carcinoma, are very rare and usually clinically aggressive. Borderline ovarian tumors are also described as tumors of low malignant potential. An illustrated 14-year-old had several months of abdominal distension and occasional constipation. Imaging demonstrated an intraperitoneal mass inseparable from the right ovary that compressed the pancreas and abdominal aorta; exploration found a mature cystic ovarian teratoma with adenocarcinoma foci measuring 28 × 22 × 14 cm.

document_sections.heading: 3.3. Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors
document_sections.content: Sex cord-stromal tumors, including thecomas, fibromas, juvenile granulosa cell tumor, and Sertoli–Leydig cell tumors, are uncommon in children and adolescents and account for approximately 5% of ovarian malignancies. Unlike epithelial and germ cell tumors, they frequently produce hormonal manifestations such as hirsutism, virilization, menstrual changes, or precocious puberty. Some are associated with genetic abnormalities; an underlying cancer-predisposition condition should always be considered.

document_sections.heading: 3.4. Imaging
document_sections.content: Transabdominal ultrasound is the primary examination for pediatric and adolescent adnexal masses. It assesses origin, size, cystic or solid consistency, side, ascites, and lymphadenopathy; Doppler evaluates vascular flow. Sonographic techniques should be interpreted with the clinical history to distinguish normal ovulatory findings from disease. Cited meta-analyses of observational studies found that combining gray-scale morphology with color Doppler performs better than morphology, spectral Doppler, or color Doppler alone. Ultrasound seeks to classify a lesion as almost certainly benign or as having a reasonable possibility of malignancy, not to establish certainty. No adnexal-mass classification is universally accepted; systems discussed are International Ovarian Tumor Analysis (IOTA) Simple Rules and Ovarian-Adnexal Reporting and Data System (O-RADS). Simple cysts are usually physiological and anechoic, without septations, solid portions, or mural nodules; they can have ≤1 peripheral calcification and no Doppler flow. Mucinous and serous cystadenomas commonly cause simple-appearing cysts. Complex cystic masses may contain nodular or papillary solid components (<50 percent), thick walls, septations (>2 to 3 mm), multiple calcifications, or mural nodules. Suddenly appearing complex masses can result from torsion, tubo-ovarian abscess, or ectopic pregnancy; persistent complex masses can reflect mature or immature teratomas or endometriomas. A primarily solid mass, defined as ≥50 percent solid components, is considered malignant until histology shows otherwise; examples include dysgerminoma, juvenile granulosa cell tumors, and Sertoli–Leydig cell tumors. Sonographic features more suggestive of malignancy are size ≥ 8 to 10 cm, multiple or bilateral lesions, solid or heterogeneous morphology including solid components > 2 cm, thick septations or papillary projections, invasion or metastases, calcifications, ascites, and increased flow. CT or MRI can further characterize a mass and assess pelvic nodes or lung and liver metastases if ultrasound does not establish its origin or it is large or suspected to be malignant.

document_sections.heading: 3.5. Laboratory Findings
document_sections.content: Potentially informative marker–tumor associations are AFP with immature teratomas, yolk sac tumors, embryonal carcinoma, and rarely Sertoli–Leydig cell tumors; LDH with dysgerminomas; β-hCG with embryonal carcinoma, non-gestational choriocarcinoma, and rarely dysgerminomas; CA-125 with malignant epithelial tumors; and inhibin A and B with juvenile granulosa cell tumors. Estradiol and testosterone are assessed when hormonal activity is suspected, such as early puberty or virilization. A marker panel improves sensitivity and specificity, but normal markers cannot exclude malignancy and raised markers can occur in benign disease; markers therefore cannot establish or eliminate a malignant diagnosis. The pediatric value of human epididymis protein 4 (HE4) remains under investigation and is less established than in adults. The role of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), more closely associated with adult cancers, is also less defined in pediatric ovarian malignancy; values vary by tumor type, age, and individual characteristics. Although the ROMA (Risk of Ovarian Malignancy Algorithm) index is used to assess ovarian tumors, differing pediatric tumor biology limits its application, and further research must establish its diagnostic accuracy and clinical usefulness. Pediatric malignancy-risk assessment requires clinical, imaging, laboratory, and histologic information alongside emerging scores. The Gynecologic Oncology Group (GOG) Staging System describes disease extent and guides treatment; Children’s Oncology Group (COG) protocols stratify pediatric risk by age, tumor type, stage, and histology; the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Staging System, chiefly used in adults, can also classify pediatric tumors by size and spread. Definitive mass diagnosis requires surgical removal and histopathology. Serial serum markers can assist postoperative surveillance for relapse. Ascites cytology and platelet assessment may also help: raised platelets are a nonspecific ovarian-mass marker and may aid acute evaluation of a twisted mass, while platelet counts generally remain normal in nonmalignant ovarian torsion. A childhood ovarian neoplasm may be the first sign of inherited cancer susceptibility, allowing genetic counseling and surveillance of patients and relatives. Associated conditions include Turner syndrome, Gorlin syndrome, Li–Fraumeni syndrome, Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, and familial breast and ovarian cancer syndrome.

document_sections.heading: 3.6. Management
document_sections.content: Surgical aims are definitive diagnosis, complete neoplasm removal, malignant staging, symptom relief, and preservation of ovarian tissue and function where possible. Gonadal function supports both fertility and normal puberty. Ovarian-conserving surgery is therefore used unless imaging and raised markers strongly suggest malignancy or an intraoperative frozen section confirms it. Because abdominal scarring may harm self-esteem and psychological well-being, treatment should be minimally invasive when feasible, including ovarian-sparing laparoscopy. Despite a recommendation to preserve ovaries for benign tumors in children and adolescents, 46–54% of these lesions undergo oophorectomy; treatment by pediatric and adolescent gynecologists is associated with fewer unnecessary oophorectomies. Suspected or confirmed malignancy calls for appropriate staging with abdominal and pelvic inspection, peritoneal lavage, biopsies of suspicious sites, and pelvic and periaortic lymph-node sampling. A management flowchart is provided.

document_sections.heading: 3.7. Differential Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Adnexal masses in young patients have a broad differential. In fetuses and neonates, alternatives include reproductive anomalies, urinary obstruction or urachal cysts, mesenteric or omental cysts, volvulus, colonic atresia, intestinal duplication, choledochal, splenic or pancreatic cysts, and lymphangioma. In children and adolescents, gynecologic possibilities include tubal and paratubal cysts, Müllerian abnormalities, tubo-ovarian abscess, pelvic inflammatory disease and other infections, endometrioma, hydrosalpinx, pyosalpinx, and ectopic pregnancy. Nongynecologic considerations particularly include peritoneal inclusion cysts, appendicitis, and appendiceal abscess. The table organizes additional gynecologic and nongynecologic differential diagnoses. Diagnostic algorithms can guide treatment; an acute abdomen from hemorrhage, torsion, inflammation, or perforation indicates urgent surgery, principally laparoscopy.

document_sections.heading: 3.8. Follow-Up
document_sections.content: Long-term follow-up after pediatric ovarian tumor surgery monitors recurrence and complications and addresses psychological effects, especially during adolescence. Appointments are generally scheduled every 3 to 6 months during the first 2 to 3 years, then annually for up to 5 years or longer. Physical examinations and relevant tumor markers are used; ultrasound, or CT or MRI when necessary, can be added for concerning symptoms or findings. Complications depend on tumor type and whether surgery was laparoscopic or open. Beyond standard surgical complications and adhesions, possible hormonal disturbance and fertility require attention. Diagnosis and surgery can cause anxiety or depression and substantially affect adolescent self-esteem. Mental-health support is important throughout short- and long-term recovery.

document_sections.heading: 4.1. Ovarian Torsion
document_sections.content: Ovarian torsion affects girls of any age at an incidence of 4.9 per 100,000. It commonly accompanies adnexal disease but can occur without it, for example with an elongated utero-ovarian ligament, particularly before puberty; associated masses are usually benign. In-utero torsion can cause ovarian necrosis followed by a calcified or sessile mass or complete disappearance. Typical manifestations are abrupt, intense unilateral lower abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and pallor; neonates and young infants may instead develop sudden marked irritability. Intermittent pain may reflect torsion without complete vascular obstruction. No particular symptom duration reliably establishes ovarian necrosis. Although progression varies individually, prolonged torsion raises the risk of substantial injury, making prompt diagnosis and treatment important for preservation. Ultrasound with Doppler is the imaging choice, but normal flow cannot exclude torsion because partial obstruction, intermittent rotation, or collateral vessels can maintain perfusion. Particularly sensitive findings include ovarian edema, altered flow, a whirlpool sign, and enlargement relative to the opposite ovary. CT and MRI are not routinely used but may help with equivocal ultrasound. Differential diagnoses include ectopic pregnancy, ruptured ovarian cyst, tubo-ovarian abscess, and appendicitis. Direct surgical visualization confirms the diagnosis. Torsion is a surgical emergency; untwisting the vascular pedicle salvages most ovaries. Laparoscopic detorsion with cystectomy and ovarian preservation is the preferred standard. Oophorectomy is rarely needed for extensive severe necrosis or a nonviable gelatinous appearance. Ovaries that appear blue or black can still regain function after detorsion, supporting ovarian preservation as initial treatment. Oophoropexy has been proposed to reduce recurrence and reproductive harm, particularly after recurrent, bilateral, or idiopathic torsion. Options include utero-ovarian ligament plication without fixation or fixation of the ovary to the uterosacral ligament or pelvic sidewall.

document_sections.heading: 4.2. Fallopian Tube Torsion
document_sections.content: Fallopian tube torsion is isolated rotation of the tube without ovarian torsion, either along its middle segment or around its supporting ligaments. Pain can be acute or chronic, generalized or nonspecific, and may accompany nausea and vomiting. Missed torsion can destroy tubal function and lead to hydrosalpinx, necrosis, or resorption. Potential contributors include hydrosalpinx, segmental tubal agenesis with proximal hydrosalpinx, broad ligament or paratubal cysts, neoplasms, ectopic pregnancy, congenital anomalies, ovarian masses, infection, abnormal peristalsis or spasm, and external lesions such as adhesions. Imaging may show a dilated tube, an adjacent normal ovary, or a cystic mass separate from the ovary. Diagnosis is generally made during surgical exploration. Detorsion can prevent irreversible ischemic damage and loss of the tube.

document_sections.heading: 4.3. Paratubal or Paraovarian Cyst Torsion
document_sections.content: Torsion of a paraovarian cyst is uncommon in children, and identifying a paraovarian cyst before surgery is difficult. Suspicion increases when imaging shows a normal ovary on the affected side and a cyst beside the uterus. Adnexal torsion risk with these cysts depends on cyst size. A twisted cyst should be excised carefully to preserve ovarian and fallopian-tube function; laparoscopic removal has demonstrated favorable outcomes. An illustrated 15-year-old had pain, fever, and vomiting beginning five days before surgery. Ultrasound identified a cyst measuring 13 × 10 × 8 cm beside an edematous left ovary without visible flow. Laparoscopy showed a large paraovarian cyst and left adnexal torsion. Overt gangrene of the ovary and tube led to laparoscopic salpingo-oophorectomy; histology found a necrotic paraovarian cyst and gangrenous ovary.

document_sections.heading: 4.4. Ruptured Hemorrhagic Ovarian Cyst
document_sections.content: A ruptured hemorrhagic cyst generally causes sudden focal, one-sided lower abdominal pain, often midway through the menstrual cycle, sometimes with intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Massive bleeding may produce shoulder or upper abdominal pain from blood beneath the diaphragm. Bleeding may stop spontaneously or cause hemodynamic instability. Self-limited cases warrant serial hemoglobin and hematocrit measurements. Unstable patients should be stabilized before surgery, often laparoscopic. Laparotomy is recommended only if the surgeon lacks pediatric laparoscopic experience or an unstable patient cannot be stabilized. An illustrated 14-year-old had acute pain and vomiting; ultrasound showed a left ovarian cystic-solid mass measuring 11 × 8 cm with disruption and free abdominal fluid. Exploratory laparotomy and left adnexectomy identified a ruptured, twisted tumor, confirmed histologically as a ruptured ovarian cystic mature teratoma.

document_sections.heading: 5. Cystectomy
document_sections.content: When benign ovarian disease needs surgery, cystectomy or solid-tumor enucleation is generally preferable to oophorectomy because it preserves more ovarian cortex. Aspiration alone is not recommended: it supplies no histopathology specimen, and cyst-fluid cytology cannot reliably rule out malignancy. Oophorectomy is generally performed when ovarian preservation is impossible or conservation leaves insufficient viable tissue. During open cystectomy, an elliptical incision along the ovarian axis is placed through thin cortex in a dependent area, avoiding the fallopian tube and fimbria ovarica. The cyst wall is separated from cortex; a base very near the stroma may require scissors or electrocautery. Intact removal is preferable. If rupture occurs, leakage must be controlled and the abdomen thoroughly cleaned to reduce contamination and complications such as pseudomyxoma peritonei or chemical peritonitis. After removal, leaving ovarian tissue open is preferred; reapproximation can provide hemostasis, while sutures on the capsule should be avoided. Multiple cysts should be approached with as few surface incisions as possible. For laparoscopic cystectomy, the ovary is steadied by grasping the utero-ovarian ligament. Intact dissection from cortex is preferred, usually with blunt dissection and sometimes electrocautery. If cystotomy becomes necessary, leakage must be controlled, contents fully aspirated, and the cavity rinsed. The wall is examined for suspicious areas, which should be dissected when possible; inseparable areas can be fulgurated. Laparoscopy-guided minilaparotomy may limit intraperitoneal spillage with large cysts.

document_sections.heading: 6. Oophorectomy
document_sections.content: Oophorectomy may be indicated for benign neoplasms unsuitable for cystectomy or partial oophorectomy, rare torsion with necrosis, ovarian malignancy, or a tubo-ovarian abscess unresponsive to antibiotics. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is preferred because, compared with laparotomy, it is associated with fewer complications, faster recovery, and lower costs. Dense adnexal adhesions, marked ovarian enlargement, or strong suspicion of malignancy may instead favor laparotomy. Robot-assisted and single-port laparoscopy remain under development, particularly in children. Regardless of approach, abdominal and pelvic lavage specimens are retained for staging should malignancy be confirmed later, and suspicious lesions found on inspection require biopsy and frozen-section assessment. Opening the broad ligament permits identification of the ureter. If the tube will be removed, lifting the ovarian vessels helps expose the nearby ureter; vessels are divided and pedicles secured 1 to 2 cm above the ovary for hemostasis and complete removal. When preserving the tube during open surgery, its ovarian-artery branches are clamped and ligated individually below and parallel to the tube. Laparoscopically, pedicles are sealed or coagulated before division. Ureteral injuries have occurred in both open and minimally invasive procedures when the ureter was inadequately identified; exposure may require opening the peritoneum and further dissection. Compared with patients retaining two ovaries, those with one ovary had a smaller ovarian-reserve quantity, such as fewer follicles, but similar reserve quality, such as pregnancy rates.

document_sections.heading: 7. Conclusions
document_sections.content: Pediatric ovarian cysts and masses call for careful surveillance and a conservative, individually tailored approach because their presentation and management differ from adult disease. Intervention is generally reserved for symptoms or concerning features. Specialized multidisciplinary care involving pediatric gynecologists, pediatric surgeons, and pediatric oncologists when malignancy is suspected can provide physical and psychological support, prevent unnecessary oophorectomies, and preserve ovarian function, hormonal balance, fertility, and overall health.
